items.title: If you are arrested
items.summary: The Constitution and criminal procedure give you basic protections from the moment of arrest.
points: You must be told the grounds of arrest (Article 22(1); CrPC 50, now BNSS 47).
You can ask police to inform a relative or friend (CrPC 50A, now BNSS 48).
You have the right to consult a lawyer of your choice.
You must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time (Article 22(2); CrPC 57, now BNSS 58).
Ask for a medical examination if you were hurt. Police must follow the D.K. Basu guidelines (Supreme Court, 1997): arrest memo, witness, entry in diary.
Do not sign blank papers. You may stay silent beyond giving basic identity details.

items.title: Filing an FIR
items.summary: Police must register an FIR when you report a cognizable offence.
points: FIR can be given orally or in writing; get a free copy (CrPC 154, now BNSS 173).
You can file a Zero FIR at any police station, even outside the area; it is then transferred.
If police refuse, send the complaint in writing to the Superintendent of Police (CrPC 154(3), now BNSS 173(4)).
You can also ask the Magistrate to order an investigation (CrPC 156(3), now BNSS 175(3)).
Lalita Kumari v. Govt of U.P. (2014): registration is mandatory for cognizable offences.

items.title: Bail basics
items.summary: Whether you can claim bail as a right depends on the type of offence.
points: In a bailable offence, bail is a right (CrPC 436, now BNSS 478).
Non-bailable offences: the court decides (CrPC 437, now BNSS 480).
Anticipatory bail can be sought if you fear arrest (CrPC 438, now BNSS 482).
Default bail may be available if the investigation is not completed within the legal time limit (CrPC 167(2), now BNSS 187). Ask a lawyer to check the exact period.

items.title: Defective product or poor service
items.summary: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers goods, services and e-commerce.
points: First complain to the seller or company in writing and keep proof.
Call the National Consumer Helpline (1915) or use consumerhelpline.gov.in.
File a case in the District Consumer Commission, online through e-Daakhil. A lawyer is not compulsory.
Time limit: generally 2 years from the cause of action (Section 69).
You can ask for refund, replacement, removal of defect and compensation. Check current fee and money limits for each Commission.

items.title: Rights of a tenant
items.summary: Rent laws differ by state. Your written agreement and state rent law decide most questions.
points: A landlord cannot evict you by force, cut water/electricity, or lock you out. Eviction needs a legal process.
Insist on a written rent agreement and receipts for rent and deposit.
For a month-to-month tenancy, termination generally needs a notice (Transfer of Property Act s.106 gives 15 days where no other rule applies). Check your state rent law.
The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is a model for states; only some states have adopted something similar.
Security deposit refund rules depend on the agreement and your state law.
items.act: Transfer of Property Act 1882; state Rent Acts

items.title: Wages, termination and workplace rights
items.summary: Labour law is being consolidated into new Labour Codes; check which rules apply to your job and state.
points: Wages must be paid on time and without illegal deductions (Payment of Wages Act / Code on Wages).
PF and ESI contributions are mandatory for covered employees; check your passbook on the EPFO portal.
Maternity benefit: 26 weeks for the first two children (Maternity Benefit Act, as amended in 2017).
Workplaces with 10 or more employees must have an Internal Committee for sexual-harassment complaints (POSH Act, 2013).
For unfair termination or unpaid dues, approach the Labour Commissioner / Labour Court. Keep appointment letter, payslips and chats as proof.
items.act: Payment of Wages Act; POSH Act 2013; Maternity Benefit Act 1961

items.title: Right to Information (RTI)
items.summary: Any citizen can ask a public authority for information.
points: Write to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the department; central application fee is Rs 10 (states differ). Persons below poverty line are exempt.
The reply is due within 30 days (48 hours if life or liberty is involved).
No reply or unsatisfactory reply: first appeal to the First Appellate Authority within 30 days.
Still unsatisfied: second appeal to the Information Commission within 90 days.
You need not give a reason for seeking information. Some information is exempt (Section 8).

items.title: Free legal services
items.summary: If you cannot afford a lawyer, the State provides one.
points: Eligible groups include women, children, SC/ST members, persons in custody, persons with disabilities, industrial workmen and persons below an income limit set by each state (Legal Services Authorities Act, Section 12).
Call NALSA helpline 15100 or visit the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in your district court complex.
Free legal aid is part of the right to equal justice (Article 39A).
Lok Adalats settle many disputes free of court fee.

items.title: Online fraud or cybercrime
items.summary: Speed matters. Report immediately so money can be frozen.
points: Call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in as soon as possible.
Inform your bank at once and ask them to block the card/account.

Under RBI customer-protection rules, your liability for unauthorised electronic transactions can be zero or limited if you report within the stated number of days. Report immediately and get a complaint number.
Save screenshots, transaction IDs, phone numbers, UPI IDs and messages.

items.title: Complaints against a bank or insurer
items.summary: Go step by step: company first, regulator next.
points: Bank: complain to the bank in writing and keep the acknowledgement. If no satisfactory reply in 30 days, file on RBI's CMS portal (RBI Ombudsman).
Insurance: complain to the insurer's grievance cell, then use IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal or the Insurance Ombudsman.
Keep policy documents, claim forms and all correspondence.
items.act: RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021; IRDAI rules

items.title: Domestic violence and harassment
items.summary: Several laws protect women from violence at home and work.
points: Helplines: 181 (Women Helpline), 112 (emergency).
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005: protection orders, residence orders and monetary relief from a Magistrate.
Cruelty by husband or relatives is an offence (IPC 498A, now BNS 85).
Maintenance for wife, children and parents (CrPC 125, now BNSS 144).
A Zero FIR can be lodged at any police station.

items.title: Senior citizens
items.summary: Parents and senior citizens can claim maintenance from children or relatives.
points: Apply to the Maintenance Tribunal under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007.
Elderline helpline: 14567.
A senior citizen can seek cancellation of a gift/transfer of property if the transferee fails to provide basic needs, if the conditions of the Act are met.
items.act: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007

items.title: Builder delay or property fraud
items.summary: Real-estate projects must be registered with the state RERA.
points: Check the project and builder on your state RERA website.
For delayed possession you can claim interest/refund by filing a complaint with the state RERA authority.
Verify title documents and encumbrance certificate before paying large sums.
